question.text: A block of mass m sits on an inclined plane whose angle θ with the horizontal is slowly increased from 0° up to 90°. The coefficients of static and kinetic friction between the block and the plane are μₛ and μₖ. Sketch how the friction force f acting on the block varies as θ increases.
conditions: block of mass m on an incline

figure.description: A block of mass m rests on an inclined plane whose angle θ with the horizontal can be increased. The friction coefficients between the block and the plane are μₛ (static) and μₖ (kinetic).

solution.approach: Friction equals mg sinθ while the block rests; once θ passes tanθ = μₛ, it drops to the kinetic value and falls further as θ increases.

steps.text: For small θ the block does not slide, so friction balances the component of weight along the incline.
steps.equation: f = mg sinθ, for 0 ≤ θ ≤ θₛ

steps.text: Friction can rise only up to its maximum static value. The block is on the verge of sliding when the incline angle reaches θₛ.
steps.equation: tanθₛ = μₛ, f_max = μₛ mg cosθₛ

steps.text: Past θₛ the block slides, so friction switches to the kinetic value, which is smaller than the static maximum because μₖ < μₛ.
steps.equation: f = μₖ mg cosθ, for θ > θₛ
steps.why_this_step: Kinetic friction is always less than the limiting static friction, so f drops suddenly at θₛ.

steps.text: As θ increases further toward 90°, cosθ keeps falling, so the kinetic friction keeps falling with it, reaching zero at θ = 90°.
steps.why_this_step: At θ = 90° the incline is vertical, the normal force is zero, and friction is proportional to the normal force.

final_answer.value: f rises as mg sinθ from 0 at θ = 0° up to the limiting value μₛ mg cosθₛ at θₛ = tan⁻¹μₛ, drops there to the smaller kinetic value μₖ mg cosθₛ, then falls further as μₖ mg cosθ down to 0 at θ = 90°.

common_mistakes.text: Drawing friction as always increasing with θ, never dropping at θₛ, by forgetting that friction switches from static to a smaller kinetic value once sliding begins.
Drawing friction as a straight line in θ instead of following sinθ then cosθ, by treating the angle dependence as linear.
